title: How the Eye Makes Pictures
description: Ray Bot traces a single beam from Umbra all the way to your retina. Follow it to understand how your eye turns light into a picture — upside down!

content.value: The lens of your eye focuses light to form a real image on the retina — but that image is actually UPSIDE DOWN and smaller than the object. Your brain is so clever that it flips the picture the right way up for you automatically. You never notice!

Object 🌳  ─▶ lens ─▶  🌳 (upside down on retina)
                        ─▶ brain flips it ─▶ 🌳 (you see it upright)

An image stays on the retina for about 1/16th of a second after the object is gone. This is called PERSISTENCE OF VISION. It is why a fast series of still pictures looks like smooth motion — it is the secret behind movies, cartoons and flip-books!
Seeing in Colour and the Dark

The retina has two kinds of light cells: CONES that detect colours (and need bright light) and RODS that work in dim light (but not colour). This is why colours fade at night — in the dark, mostly your rods are working, so everything looks grey.
Some animals see differently: many are colour-blind, while bees can even see ultraviolet light we cannot. Every eye is tuned to its owner's world.

Key Takeaway: The lens forms an upside-down image on the retina which the brain corrects. Persistence of vision makes movies possible, and rods (dim light) plus cones (colour) let us see in different conditions.

quiz.question: The image formed on the retina is…
options: upside down and smaller, then corrected by the brain
the same as a mirror image
quiz.explain: The lens makes an inverted (upside-down), smaller image on the retina; the brain flips it so you see it upright.

quiz.question: Persistence of vision means an image stays on the retina for about…
options: 1/16th of a second after the object is gone
quiz.explain: The retina holds an image for roughly 1/16 s, which lets rapid still frames look like smooth motion in films.

quiz.question: Why do colours look faded in very dim light?
options: In dim light mainly the rods work, and rods do not detect colour
quiz.explain: Cones need bright light to detect colour. In the dark, mostly rods work, so we see shapes but little colour.
